strengths: Identifies a novel and non-trivial theoretical connection between two previously separate lines of Schrödinger Bridge solvers (IPF and IMF), showing that the practical bidirectional IMF heuristic used in DSBM/ASBM is secretly composed of IPF and IMF projections. This is a genuine conceptual insight with potential to unify disparate strands of SB literature.

Provides a rigorous, non-trivial theoretical proof of quantitative (exponential) convergence for the 1D Gaussian case, including a careful treatment of interactions between forward/reverse KL-decreasing projections, with detailed appendix derivations (Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2, and supporting lemmas).

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of settings: closed-form high-dimensional Gaussians, 2D toy examples, the standard SB benchmark, and real image datasets (colored MNIST, CelebA), using two different practical algorithms (DSBM and ASBM) based on diffusion models and GANs respectively.
The experiments convincingly show that IPMF converges from a broader class of starting processes than either pure IPF or pure IMF would allow, supporting the main theoretical/conceptual claim.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, architectures, and training details for all experiments are provided in the appendix.

Discussion connects the findings to practically important issues (e.g., error accumulation in rectified flow distillation, foundational generative models), suggesting broader relevance beyond the immediate SB community.
weaknesses: The formal convergence theory is restricted to a fairly narrow setting (1D Gaussians, and for discrete time only N=1 intermediate point); the general multivariate/non-Gaussian convergence claim remains a conjecture supported only empirically, which the authors themselves acknowledge as a limitation.

The core contribution is largely a reinterpretation/decomposition of an existing widely-used heuristic (bidirectional IMF) rather than a new algorithm; the practical training procedure does not change from what practitioners already do, somewhat limiting the practical novelty despite the theoretical value.

On real-world datasets (CelebA, colored MNIST) and even the SB benchmark at low epsilon, the differences between starting processes are sometimes inconsistent with the 'more general convergence' narrative (e.g., IPF/Independent starting processes underperform at small epsilon on the benchmark), which slightly undercuts the strength of the generalization claim.

Limited baseline comparison in the unpaired translation experiments — essentially only DSBM/ASBM variants under different initializations are compared, with only SF2M-Sink as an external baseline in the benchmark table; broader comparison to other SB or non-SB unpaired translation methods is missing.

The paper is dense and mathematically heavy, which may reduce accessibility; more intuitive exposition or visual explanation of why IPF and IMF projections interact as claimed would strengthen clarity for a broader audience.

Quantitative real-data results (FID, CMMD) across different starting processes are quite close to each other in absolute terms, making it hard to assess how much the choice of starting process (and hence the IPMF framing) practically matters versus other confounds like network architecture or training length.

strengths: Provides a novel and insightful theoretical connection between the previously separate IPF and IMF procedures, explaining why the empirically successful 'bidirectional IMF' heuristic used in DSBM/ASBM actually secretly performs IPF projections. This is a nontrivial conceptual unification of two major lines of work on Schrödinger Bridges.

Rigorous theoretical analysis for the 1D (and multi-dim discrete N=1) Gaussian case, including a clean and general lemma (Lemma 3.1) showing any Gaussian joint is an entropic OT plan for some transport cost, and a quantitative exponential convergence theorem (Thm 3.2) with detailed, careful proofs in the appendix (contraction arguments for both IMF and IPF sub-steps).

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of settings: closed-form high-dimensional Gaussians, 2D toy Swiss-roll example, the standard SB benchmark (varying D and epsilon), and two real image translation tasks (colored MNIST, CelebA), using both the diffusion-based (DSBM) and GAN-based (ASBM) practical algorithms.
Good reproducibility: hyperparameters, architectures, and training details are thoroughly documented in the appendix, and theoretical derivations are fully included.

The reframing has some potential broader implications for distillation methods like rectified flows, offering a principled way to think about correcting error accumulation in one-directional procedures.
weaknesses: The rigorous convergence proof only covers the 1D Gaussian (or discrete-time with a single intermediate point) case; the central claim that IPMF converges 'under more general settings' from arbitrary starting processes is only a conjecture supported by experiments, not proven in general — this is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation but tempers the strength of the main claim.

The empirical evidence for the central hypothesis is somewhat mixed: in the SB benchmark (Table 1/2) and Gaussian experiments, the IPF-starting and Independent starting processes sometimes perform comparably to or even better than the IMF-starting process, which slightly muddies the narrative that all initializations converge equally well/fast.

No new algorithm or practical method is proposed — the paper reinterprets existing DSBM/ASBM training procedures rather than introducing an improved algorithm, so the practical impact (e.g., in terms of new SOTA results or efficiency gains) is limited relative to the theoretical contribution.

The paper is notation-heavy and dense, which may hinder accessibility for readers not already deeply familiar with IPF/IMF/DSBM/ASBM literature; the discrete vs. continuous time dual exposition (with most technical content pushed to the appendix) adds to the complexity.
The discussion of potential impact on rectified-flow distillation methods (Section 5) is largely speculative and not empirically tested in the paper.

Some experimental comparisons (e.g. Colored MNIST, CelebA) are primarily qualitative/illustrative and do not strongly quantify the specific benefit of the IPMF framing over standard bidirectional IMF training as already practiced.

strengths: Provides a clear and elegant theoretical explanation for a widely-used but previously ad-hoc heuristic (bidirectional/alternating forward-backward IMF used in DSBM and ASBM), showing it secretly implements IPF projections interleaved with IMF projections, unifying two previously separate lines of work (IPF/Sinkhorn and IMF/rectified-flow-style methods) under a single IPMF framework.

Rigorous theoretical convergence analysis for the Gaussian case, including a novel characterization of Gaussian plans as entropic OT solutions (optimality matrix formalism) and exponential convergence proofs under several settings (D=1, and D>1 with large epsilon), with detailed and careful proofs in the appendix.

Extensive empirical validation spanning multiple regimes: high-dimensional Gaussians (closed-form updates), 2D toy distributions, the standard SB benchmark across dimensions and volatilities, and real image data (colored MNIST, CelebA), consistently supporting the central conjecture that IPMF converges from a much broader class of initializations than IPF or IMF alone.

The unification has potential downstream significance, e.g., suggesting how rectified-flow-style distillation techniques (which correspond to one-directional IMF) could be modified to avoid error accumulation, connecting to practically important models like Stable Diffusion 3.
The paper is transparent about its main limitation (general convergence beyond Gaussians is conjectured, not proven) and frames this appropriately as future work rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The convergence guarantee is restricted to the Gaussian setting and, even there, only for the D>1 case under a restrictive 'large epsilon' condition; the general convergence claim for arbitrary distributions remains a conjecture only supported empirically, which somewhat limits the theoretical completeness relative to the strength of the claims made in the abstract/intro.

The main contribution is primarily explanatory/theoretical (re-interpreting an existing practical heuristic) rather than introducing a new algorithm or improving performance; the paper does not show IPMF (via different starting processes) meaningfully outperforming standard DSBM/ASBM/IMF in the benchmark tables (Table 1/2), and in several high-epsilon, high-dimension settings the proposed variants are substantially worse than baselines like SF2M-Sink.

The real-data experiments (colored MNIST, CelebA) are largely qualitative and illustrative (visual samples, FID/CMMD/MSE trends over IPMF iterations) rather than rigorously demonstrating a quantitative advantage from the IPMF perspective; different starting processes trade off fidelity vs. content preservation without a clear recommendation or ablation isolating the effect of the theoretical insight.

No sensitivity/ablation analysis on key hyperparameters such as number of discretization points N, choice of epsilon relative to theoretical convergence conditions, or robustness of the convergence rate constants (alpha, beta) in practice.

Presentation is extremely dense with heavy notation and lengthy appendix proofs, which may hinder accessibility of the core insight for a broad audience; the main paper text is compressed into background/notation-heavy setup with relatively limited discussion of practical implications or algorithmic recommendations beyond the empirical illustrations.
